neighbours.label: how a substance enters or is put on the body: its route of administration (under the tongue, through the skin, applied to a wound, by mouth)
fire: These lozenges dissolve under the tongue for sublingual absorption.
Nicotine patches release the drug slowly through the skin over a day.
Zinc is considered safe when swallowed or applied to wounds in small amounts.
The ointment is applied directly to the affected skin twice daily.
Patients received the hormone by a transdermal gel rubbed on the arm.
Caffeine can be absorbed through the gums from a chewing strip.
The antibiotic drops are placed in the ear canal with a dropper.
Aspirin was given orally or as a rectal suppository in the trial.
quiet: These lozenges come in a tin and taste faintly of lemon and honey.
Nicotine is a chemical that is found in the leaves of tobacco.
Zinc is a metal that is mined in Peru, China and Australia.
The ointment costs ten dollars and is made in a small factory.
Patients who received the hormone were older and mostly lived in cities.
Caffeine raises alertness in most people within about half an hour.
The antibiotic was discovered in 1948 by a team in Italy.
Aspirin sales rose in the trial year and doctors wrote about it.

notes: A shared pattern for the card's list ('Subling-ual', 'Intratym-panic', ' skin', ' applied', ' tablets'). Probes: 0.45-0.79 on routes, under 0.15 on other facts about the same substances. The fire items use routes not on the card (transdermal, gums, ear canal, rectal).
